title: {{NAME}} and the Cup at the Top of the World
moral: Pride in your team is far sweeter than pride in yourself alone.

pages.content: The Pinnacle Cup was played at the highest natural plateau in the known world, a flat-topped mountain so old that the rock underfoot had been worn smooth by millions of years of wind and weather into something that felt, when you ran on it, like polished marble wrapped in the faintest layer of grass. The pitch markings had been scratched into the stone centuries ago, their white lines refilled before each tournament by a Triceratops named Burr who took this duty extremely seriously and had opinions about line width. {{NAME}} arrived as captain of the Irongate Royals, a team that included Princess Nara at centre-back, a defender so composed under pressure that opposing strikers sometimes lost their nerve simply from the quality of her stare. Their striker was a young Gallimimus named Flint, quick as mercury and twice as unpredictable, who scored goals that defied explanation and then seemed surprised about it. The opposing team, the Basalt Eagles, were defending champions. They were very good and they knew it, which is always the most difficult combination to play against.

pages.content: The Basalt Eagles' captain was a Pterosaur named Gale whose wingspan during throw-ins technically exceeded the pitch boundary rules, a point that Burr the line-maintenance Triceratops had filed a written complaint about, which had been politely noted and then set aside. Gale was also brilliant, a playmaker who saw the game three moves ahead with the elevated perspective of a creature who spent half their time above it. Before the match, Gale found {{NAME}} at the water station and said, with a directness that was almost admirable, 'You are shorter than your reputation.' {{NAME}} considered this. 'You have a larger wingspan than the rules allow,' he replied. Gale clicked her beak, which {{NAME}} chose to interpret as a smile. 'Fair,' she said. They shook hands, or rather hand and wing, and went back to their teams. In the dugout, Princess Nara watched this exchange with raised eyebrows. 'Did you just make friends with the opposing captain?' she asked. 'I think so,' said {{NAME}}. 'That's going to make it more interesting,' said Flint, eating something fibrous with great enthusiasm.

pages.content: The first half was as difficult as expected. The Basalt Eagles were surgical, their passes precise and swift, their movement choreographed through years of playing together. They went one-nil up with a header from a defender who had simply outjumped everyone, including Flint who could jump to a height that should, by rights, have been enough. The Royals were behind and twenty minutes from the interval. {{NAME}} called a quiet word with his team in a tight circle near the halfway line, not a tactical talk, something simpler. 'We know each other,' he said. 'They play a system. We play each other. Nara, you'll see the gap before I call for it. Flint, stop aiming. When you aim you think. When you don't aim, you score.' Flint looked at his own feet thoughtfully. 'That is genuinely how it works,' he said, with the mild surprise of someone discovering something they have always known. The equaliser came eight minutes before half time, Nara finding {{NAME}} in a gap that had not existed a half-second earlier, {{NAME}} laying it into Flint's path without breaking stride, and Flint not aiming and scoring magnificently.

pages.content: The winner came in the last two minutes, and it was not the goal anyone had scripted. The Eagles had pressed high, sensing the draw was not enough, and left the space behind them vast and empty as a meadow at dawn. Princess Nara, who never crossed halfway in normal play, looked at that space, looked at {{NAME}}, and went. She ran the length of the pitch with a composure so complete it looked almost like walking, received {{NAME}}'s through ball on her left foot, and placed it in the far corner with the unhurried precision of someone who has been waiting for exactly this moment and is not remotely surprised it has arrived. The Pinnacle Cup audience, a great crowd of dinosaurs and humans clustered at the plateau's edge, made a sound that the mountain itself seemed to lean into. Gale, to her considerable credit, was the first to find Nara afterward. 'That,' the Pterosaur said, in tones of genuine appreciation, 'was the best goal scored in this tournament in thirty years.' Nara accepted this with a nod that was, for once, not at all composed but very simply happy.

pages.content: The Pinnacle Cup was a tall thing, taller than {{NAME}} had expected, with the names of every winning team engraved in its base going back to a time when the lettering was in languages nobody spoke anymore. The Royals took it in turns to hold it, including Burr the line-maintenance Triceratops who was not technically on the team but who had clearly earned it. {{NAME}} held it last, and then, without planning to, passed it immediately to Princess Nara, who looked at him for a moment with an expression he could not fully read, and then looked at the cup, and held it up with both hands. The plateau crowd cheered again. Gale sat nearby, watching, and her expression was the look of someone who has been beaten by something excellent and has decided to find this satisfying rather than disappointing. {{NAME}} sat on the ancient stone pitch and felt the mountain through his cleats, steady and patient and very old. Flint sat beside him and ate something else fibrous. 'Good game,' Flint said. 'Very good game,' said {{NAME}}. 'We should do this every year,' said Flint. 'We probably have to qualify,' said {{NAME}}. 'That part,' said Flint cheerfully, 'I'm not worried about.'
